Crossed model weights across the levels of a factor

Source: R/bnec_group.R
crossed_group_weights.Rd

The weight of every combination of per-level models, and the two readings of that table which answer different questions.

crossed_group_weights(object, pooled = NULL)

Arguments

object

An object of class bayesnecgroupfit.

pooled

Optionally, a fit of the same model set to the whole data set, ignoring the factor, as returned by bnec. Used to answer whether the factor matters at all — see Details.

Value

A list with the per-level weight vectors, the unrestricted best combination and its weight, the diagonal weights over the models common to every level, and — if pooled was given — the grouped-versus-pooled WAIC comparison.

Details

Levels partition the data disjointly and share no parameters, so elpd is additive across them: elpd(m_1, ..., m_G) = sum_g elpd_g(m_g). Under pseudo-BMA the crossed weight of a combination is proportional to the product of its per-level weights, so the whole table follows from the per-level vectors and never has to be materialised — which matters, because with 23 models and G levels it has 23^G cells.

This identity is specific to pseudo-BMA, the package default, and crossed_group_weights() enforces it rather than assuming it: a fit built with any other weighting method is refused, because there is no correct crossed table to return for one. Stacking optimises a different objective whose solution is not generally an outer product; stacked crossed weights would require the full pointwise matrix and are not computed here. The same caveat applies to crossed_weights for hurdle fits, for the same reason.

Two readings, both useful

The unrestricted maximum picks the best model for each level independently, and will typically assign different equations to different levels. That is the direct answer to the question this function exists for: whether the functional form of the response changes across levels.

The diagonal maximum, w_m proportional to prod_g w_gm, is a comparison of common-form models: which single equation best describes every level. bayesnec could not answer that before, and it is often the question a reader of the analysis actually has.

Does the factor matter at all?

Pass pooled — a bnec fit of the same model set to the whole data set, with the factor ignored — and the same additivity gives the third reading. A pooled fit is scored on exactly the same observations as the levels together are, so their information criteria are directly comparable: the grouped WAIC is the sum over levels of the best model's WAIC, and the difference against the pooled fit's is a like-for-like comparison. A negative diff favours the pooled fit, a positive one the grouped fit.

The comparison is on WAIC because that is what bayesnec stores on every fit. A standard error for the difference needs the pointwise values, and those are kept only on a single-model fit. A bayesmanecfit stores its component fits as they were before expand_nec() attached their criteria, so it carries each model's WAIC point estimate in mod_stats and none of the pointwise values.

So se_diff is reported when every level, and the pooled fit, settled on a single model, and is NA whenever any of them is model-averaged — in which case the difference is a point estimate with no uncertainty attached, which is worth remembering before reading much into a small one. Where the values are present the observations are additionally checked to line up before anything is computed.

Note this compares the best model per level against the best pooled model, not the model-averaged predictions of either. Model averaging is within level by construction, and the averaged predictive density is not the weighted sum of the components'.

See also

bnec_group, crossed_weights

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
library(bayesnec)
crossed_group_weights(fit)
} # }
